newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran says has no intention to start war with U.S.
newsitem.headline: Iran says has no intention to start war with U.S.

text.p: Iran has no intention of starting a war with the United States, but if attacked Tehran would turn the Gulf into a "slaughterhouse" for American forces, Iran's Revolutionary Guards commander was quoted as saying on Sunday.

"Let me send a clear message to the Americans -- The Persian Gulf is our region. They have to leave our region. We have vital interests in the Persian Gulf and we are going to defend our interests," Major General Mohsen Rezaie said in an interview with the English-language Kayhan International newspaper.

"Iran will never start any war, but if the Americans one day decide to attack us, then they would have committed suicide. We will turn the region into a slaughterhouse for them. There is no place better than the Persian Gulf to destroy America's might.
"However, I don't think the Americans are after a military confrontation with the strongest power in the Persian Gulf," Rezaie added.
He reiterated Iran's denial of U.S. press reports that Tehran was linked to the bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen in Khobar in eastern Saudi Arabia last year.
"The Americans cannot have any evidence against Iran. We have nothing to do with such bombings," he said.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said during a visit to the Gulf this month that the United States was not headed towards a clash with Iran unless Tehran started it and warned Iran against any attempt to halt shipping in the oil-rich Gulf.

The United States accuses Iran of sponsoring state "terrorism" -- a charge Iran denies -- and has expressed concern since the 1991 Gulf War about what it describes as Iran's growing military capability and its aims in the region.
Iran opposes the U.S. military presence in the Gulf and says Washington falsely accuses it of threatening regional security in order to scare its Gulf Arab allies into buying more weapons.

Rezaie said Iran was ready to sign defence and security pacts with its Arab neighbours -- six oil-rich states that are deeply suspicious of Iran's arms programme and accuse it of interfering in their internal affairs.
"We are prepared to cope with any foreign threat and protect our borders. We have renovated our defence industries and we are producing most of the weapons we need," Rezaie said.

"We are now producing advanced anti-tank rockets as well as short-range and medium-range missiles. I do confirm that we are seeking to expand our defence capability but have no desire to acquire banned weapons such as nuclear bombs or chemical weapons," he added.

U.S. army General Binford Peay, who heads the U.S. Central Command with responsibility for American forces in the volatile Gulf, said on Thursday Iran was moving closer to nuclear weapons capability and is likely to have such arms at or shortly after the turn of the century.

He voiced concern that Iran's current conventional buildup of submarines and cruise missiles might spark an accidental confrontation in the Gulf, but said that both the U.S. and Iranian militaries were trying to assure that such a clash did not occur in the tense region.
